**THE PROPOSED CLASS CANNOT BE CERTIFIED BECAUSE INDIVIDUAL DAMAGES QUESTIONS WOULD OVERWHELM COMMON QUESTIONS.**

**A. Plaintiffs must prove predominance.**

Plaintiffs, as the parties seeking certification, bear the burden of showing that Rule 23 is satisfied. *Oshana v. Coca-Cola Co.*, 472 F.3d 506, 513 (7th Cir. 2006). They must do so by a preponderance of the evidence. *Messner v. Northshore Univ. HealthSystem*, 669 F.3d 802, 811 (7th Cir. 2012). A court may not simply accept the complaint's allegations; it must resolve the disputes that bear on certification, even when they overlap with the merits. *Szabo v. Bridgeport Machs., Inc.*, 249 F.3d 672, 675–77 (7th Cir. 2001). Rule 23(b)(3) further demands a rigorous inquiry into whether common questions predominate. *Comcast Corp. v. Behrend*, 569 U.S. 27, 33–34 (2013). A question is individual when class members must present evidence that varies from member to member to make a prima facie showing; it is common when the same evidence will suffice for each. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815.

**B. Damages that must be tried member by member defeat predominance.**

Predominance fails where plaintiffs offer no sound method of measuring damages across the class and individual calculations would therefore overwhelm common questions. *Comcast*, 569 U.S. at 34. Any proposed model must also measure only those damages attributable to plaintiffs' theory of liability. *Id.* at 35.

This Court enforces these requirements. In *Parko v. Shell Oil Co.*, 739 F.3d 1083, 1085–87 (7th Cir. 2014), it reversed certification where the district court had not adequately tested whether plaintiffs' account of injury and damages was realistic in light of differences among class members' properties and the defendants' counterarguments. A common question about the defendants' conduct did not end the inquiry. *Id.* at 1085–86. And in *Espenscheid v. DirectSat USA, LLC*, 705 F.3d 770, 773–76 (7th Cir. 2013), the Court affirmed decertification of wage-and-hour classes in which damages varied among some 2,300 workers and plaintiffs had no feasible way to determine them short of individualized proceedings. Testimony from selected class members could not fill the gap without a showing that the sample was representative. *Id.* at 774–76; *see also Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes*, 564 U.S. 338, 367 (2011) (rejecting "Trial by Formula").

Individualized inquiries into whether a class member was harmed, or whether the defendant is liable to that member, likewise weigh against certification. *Cf. Oshana*, 472 F.3d at 514 (affirming denial of certification where countless proposed members could not show damage caused by the challenged conduct); *Howland v. First Am. Title Ins. Co.*, 672 F.3d 525, 532–34 (7th Cir. 2012) (affirming denial where liability turned on transaction-specific assessments).

**C. The general rule regarding damages does not save this class.**

Individualized damages, standing alone, do not necessarily preclude certification. *Messner*, 669 F.3d at 815; *see Butler v. Sears, Roebuck & Co.*, 727 F.3d 796, 801 (7th Cir. 2013) (class members need not have identical damages). But that principle does not relieve plaintiffs of showing that common questions predominate in the case they actually propose to try. *Butler* emphasized that certification there was for determining liability, leaving damages for later proceedings if necessary. 727 F.3d at 800–01. It does not permit a court to disregard individual inquiries that would consume the litigation. *Espenscheid* demonstrates the consequence when plaintiffs lack a workable means of resolving them. 705 F.3d at 773–76.

That is the case here. Each member's damages turn on [identify member-specific facts, such as purchase history, actual loss, causation, offsets, and mitigation]. Plaintiffs have offered [no classwide damages model / a model that fails to account for these variables]. Resolving these questions would require a series of mini-trials in which Defendant is entitled to contest each claim with member-specific evidence. *See Wal-Mart*, 564 U.S. at 367 (a class cannot be certified on the premise that the defendant will be unable to litigate its defenses to individual claims). Bifurcating damages would not eliminate those trials; it would merely postpone them. Certification under Rule 23(b)(3) should be denied.
